messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Hairdresser
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Photos): Related photos, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Karim's Story

Karim was thirty-four when the diagnosis came back. The oncologist had used the word "lymphoma" in a small beige room at Massachusetts General Hospital, and Karim remembered the smell of the place—antiseptic and something underneath it, something organic and wrong—more clearly than he remembered the doctor's exact words. What he did hold onto was the certainty that he was going to die. Not the statistical likelihood of survival that the doctor had cited, but the absolute knowledge in his chest that his body was betraying him, that the cells multiplying inside him were proof that he could no longer trust anything his own body told him.

The chemotherapy lasted eight months. Karim continued working at his salon in Cambridge for the first three rounds, arriving in the morning with a scarf tied carefully around his head after his hair began to fall out in clumps. His regular clients asked what was wrong; he told them he had an infection. The nausea was constant. The pain moved—sometimes in his abdomen, sometimes in his chest, sometimes radiating down his left arm in a way that made him certain the cancer had spread. He would feel a sharp sensation and his mind would spiral: *it's everywhere, it's in my lungs, it's in my brain*. His body had become a landscape of threat, and he had no way to read its signals anymore. A normal ache could mean nothing, or it could mean death. There was no way to know.

By the time he finished treatment at thirty-five, Karim had achieved remission. The scans were clear. The oncologist used words like "excellent prognosis" and "long-term survival." But something had broken in the space between his mind and his body, and it did not repair itself with the disappearance of the cancer cells.

Now, three years later, Karim lives in a state of constant vigilance. His body feels as though it is always braced for collapse. Even in the mornings when he wakes up feeling fine, there is a baseline tension in his shoulders and chest, a readiness for the next catastrophe. He has come to believe that this tension itself is dangerous—that his nervous system is malfunctioning, that he is losing his grip on reality. The idea that he might be going crazy frightens him more than the cancer ever did.

The triggers are specific and relentless. Photographs of himself from before the diagnosis—particularly ones from the salon, where he is smiling, unaware—create an immediate surge of dread and anger. He cannot explain it rationally, but seeing his own face from that time feels like looking at a ghost. He has deleted most of them from his phone. When he wakes from nightmares, he lies in bed for hours in the dark, afraid to move, afraid that any change in his body's state might signal something ominous. The dreams are not always about cancer; sometimes they are about the hospital, the smell of it, the feeling of powerlessness. He wakes gasping, and the panic does not fade quickly.

Medical appointments have become nearly impossible. Last month, his primary care doctor wanted to do routine blood work. Karim went to the lab, sat in the waiting room, and felt such an overwhelming surge of terror that he left without being seen. The thought of having his blood drawn—of his body being punctured, of results that might change everything—was intolerable. He has begun to avoid these appointments entirely, which means he has not had his annual physical in two years. This avoidance has consequences: his doctor has stopped calling, which Karim interprets as abandonment, which confirms his fear that his body is too damaged, too unreliable, for anyone to care for.

At the salon, his work has suffered. He used to take pride in his precision with color and cut, but his hands shake now. Sometimes, mid-appointment, a sharp pain will shoot through his chest and he will freeze, convinced that this is the moment, that the cancer has returned. His clients have noticed. Some have begun requesting other stylists. The owner has asked, gently, if everything is okay. Karim has not told him the truth.

What finally brought Karim to seek help was a moment three weeks ago when he woke from a nightmare and found himself unable to distinguish between the dream and waking reality. He lay in bed and could smell the hospital—that same antiseptic and decay—even though he was in his bedroom. The pain in his abdomen that had haunted him during treatment suddenly returned, vivid and localized, even though he knew logically that nothing was wrong. He sat on the edge of his bed for an hour, trembling, unable to trust his own perceptions. When it finally passed, he was struck by a thought that terrified him more than any symptom: *I am losing my mind. My own body has become my enemy, and I cannot trust anything it tells me anymore.*
